statute_title: Operating Under the Influence of an Intoxicant
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first/second); Class C Felony (third within 15 years or with prior felony DUI)
elements: Defendant operated or drove a motor vehicle or aircraft
Or operated a watercraft
While under the influence of an intoxicant
Or with a BAC of .08 or higher
mandatory_minimum: 72 hours and $1,500 fine (first); 20 days and $3,000 fine (second); 60 days and $4,000 fine (third)
enhancements: BAC .15 or higher (doubled mandatory minimum jail time)
Refusal to submit to chemical test (enhanced penalties)
Third offense within 15 years (Class C Felony)
Prior felony DUI conviction (Class C Felony)
notes: Alaska has some of the strictest DUI laws. Lookback period is 15 years. Felony DUI on third offense within lookback or with prior felony DUI. Ignition interlock required.

statute_title: Operating Under the Influence — First Offense
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
While under the influence of an intoxicant or with BAC .08+
No prior DUI convictions within 15 years
enhancements: BAC .15 or higher (minimum 72 hours doubled to 144 hours)
Refusal to submit to chemical test
notes: License revocation 90 days minimum. Ignition interlock device for 6 months after revocation. Must complete alcohol screening and substance abuse education course.

statute_title: Operating Under the Influence — Repeat Offense
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (second); Class C Felony (third within 15 years)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated or with BAC .08+
One or more prior DUI convictions within 15 years
mandatory_minimum: 20 days and $3,000 fine (second); 60 days and $4,000 fine (third); 120 days and $5,000 fine (fourth); 240 days and $6,000 fine (fifth); 360 days and $7,000 fine (sixth+)
enhancements: Refusal to submit to chemical test
notes: 15-year lookback period. Third offense is a Class C Felony. Permanent license revocation possible for multiple offenses. Vehicle forfeiture after third offense.

statute_title: Operating Under the Influence — Controlled Substance
offense_class: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
penalty_min: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
penalty_max: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
fine_max: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle
While under the influence of a controlled substance
Or under the combined influence of an intoxicant and controlled substance
To a degree that renders the person incapable of driving safely
mandatory_minimum: Same as alcohol DUI by offense count
enhancements: Combined influence of alcohol and drugs
notes: Same statute covers alcohol and drug impairment. No per se limit for drugs — must prove actual impairment. Includes prescription medications.

elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle
In a manner that creates a substantial and unjustifiable risk of harm
To a person or property
notes: Common plea-down from DUI charges. 10 points on driving record. License suspension for 30-90 days possible.

statute_title: Duty to Stop at Scene — Injury or Death
offense_class: Class A Felony (death); Class C Felony (injury); Class A Misdemeanor (property damage only under AS 28.35.050)
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
Accident resulted in injury, death, or property damage
Defendant failed to immediately stop at the scene
Defendant failed to give name, address, and vehicle registration and render aid
notes: Failure to stop at a scene involving death is among the most serious traffic offenses. Property damage only is covered under AS 28.35.050.

statute_title: Murder — Second Degree (DUI resulting in death)
offense_class: Class A Felony (under depraved indifference theory); Unclassified Felony (with prior DUI convictions)
elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle while intoxicated
Defendant's conduct caused the death of another person
Under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life
notes: Alaska does not have a specific vehicular homicide statute. DUI deaths are prosecuted under the general murder or manslaughter statutes depending on the level of culpability.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
By criminal negligence or reckless conduct
While operating a motor vehicle
notes: No separate vehicular manslaughter statute — charged under general manslaughter. Reckless conduct while driving that results in death.

statute_title: Driving While License Canceled, Suspended, or Revoked
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class A Misdemeanor with enhanced penalties (subsequent)
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a highway or vehicular way
While license was suspended, revoked, or canceled
Defendant had knowledge or notice of the suspension
enhancements: Prior convictions for driving on suspended
notes: Enhanced penalties when suspension was DUI-related. Additional suspension period added to existing suspension.

statute_title: Failure to Stop at Direction of a Peace Officer
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (basic); Class C Felony (reckless eluding)
elements: A peace officer signaled the defendant to stop
Defendant knowingly failed to stop as directed
Officer was in uniform and operating a marked vehicle
enhancements: Reckless driving while eluding (Class C Felony under AS 11.56.730)
notes: Eluding with reckless driving is charged under AS 11.56.730 as a separate felony. Vehicle may be impounded.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving a Controlled Substance — Fourth Degree
offense_class: Class C Felony (Schedule IA/IIA); Class A Misdemeanor (Schedule IIIA-VIA small amounts)
penalty_max: 5 years (Class C Felony); 1 year (Class A Misdemeanor)
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
Without lawful authority or prescription
Substance is listed in Alaska's controlled substance schedules
notes: Alaska's controlled substance laws use degrees (First through Sixth) rather than categories. Severity depends on substance and amount.

offense_class: Legal (1 oz or less for adults 21+); Class B Misdemeanor (minor in possession); Class A Misdemeanor (public consumption)
penalty_max: 90 days (Class B Misdemeanor); 1 year (Class A Misdemeanor)
elements: For criminal charges: defendant possessed marijuana in excess of legal limits
Or consumed marijuana in a public place
Or defendant was under 21 years of age
enhancements: Possession over 1 oz but under 4 oz (violation)
Possession of 4+ oz (Class C Felony under AS 11.71.040)
notes: Alaska legalized recreational marijuana in 2014. Adults 21+ may possess up to 1 oz and grow up to 6 plants (3 mature). Over 4 oz is a felony. Under 21 is still criminal.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving Controlled Substance — Fourth Degree (Cocaine)
elements: Defendant possessed cocaine
Cocaine is a Schedule IIA controlled substance in Alaska
Possession was without lawful authority
enhancements: Amount over 1 gram (may support higher degree charge)
notes: Any amount of cocaine possession is a Class C Felony in Alaska. Larger amounts elevate to third or second degree misconduct.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving Controlled Substance — Fourth Degree (Methamphetamine)
elements: Defendant possessed methamphetamine
Methamphetamine is a Schedule IIA controlled substance
Possession was without lawful authority
notes: Any amount of meth possession is a Class C Felony. Manufacturing is a more serious offense under AS 11.71.020 or AS 11.71.030.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving a Controlled Substance — First Degree
elements: Defendant manufactured, delivered, or possessed with intent to deliver
A Schedule IA or IIA controlled substance
In a quantity meeting trafficking thresholds
notes: Unclassified Felony carries the most severe penalties. Presumptive sentencing applies. Thresholds vary by substance.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving a Controlled Substance — Second Degree
elements: Defendant manufactured, delivered, or possessed with intent to deliver
A controlled substance listed in Schedule IA, IIA, IIIA, or IVA
notes: Second-degree covers distribution of Schedule IA-IVA substances that doesn't meet first-degree thresholds.

offense_class: Class A Felony (Schedule IA/IIA); Class B Felony (Schedule IIIA-IVA)
elements: Defendant manufactured, compounded, or processed a controlled substance
Without lawful authority
notes: Manufacturing methamphetamine is treated especially seriously. Cleanup costs may be assessed as restitution.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving Controlled Substance — Fifth Degree (Paraphernalia)
elements: Defendant possessed drug paraphernalia
With intent to use it for ingesting, inhaling, or injecting a controlled substance
enhancements: Delivery of paraphernalia to a minor
notes: Marijuana paraphernalia is legal for adults 21+ under AS 17.38. Paraphernalia for other drugs remains criminal.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving a Controlled Substance — Third Degree
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
With intent to manufacture or deliver
Without lawful authority
enhancements: Near a school or recreation center
notes: Intent inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, and other circumstantial evidence. Third-degree covers possession with intent for lower schedule substances.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
With intent to cause the death
The conduct was premeditated
Or directed at a person under 16 under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference
mandatory_minimum: 20 years (presumptive for first felony offender); 30 years (aggravated first degree)
enhancements: Victim was a peace officer or firefighter
Committed during commission of specified felonies
notes: Alaska abolished the death penalty in 1957. Maximum sentence is 99 years. Presumptive sentencing guidelines apply.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
With intent to cause serious physical injury
Or under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life
Or during commission of arson, kidnapping, sexual assault, robbery, or escape
enhancements: Felony murder (during commission of specified felony)
notes: Covers intentional killing without premeditation, depraved indifference murder, and felony murder.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
Under circumstances that would otherwise constitute murder
Acting under the influence of extreme emotional disturbance
For which there was a reasonable explanation
notes: Alaska follows the Model Penal Code approach with extreme emotional disturbance rather than traditional heat-of-passion doctrine.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
By reckless conduct
Defendant was aware of and consciously disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk
notes: Reckless manslaughter covers what most states call involuntary manslaughter. Criminally negligent homicide (AS 11.41.130) is a Class B Felony for lesser culpability.

elements: Defendant recklessly caused serious physical injury to another by means of a dangerous instrument
Or intentionally caused serious physical injury by any means
notes: First-degree assault is Alaska's equivalent of aggravated assault. Serious physical injury means injury creating substantial risk of death, or causing protracted impairment.

elements: Defendant recklessly caused physical injury to another person
Or with criminal negligence caused physical injury by means of a dangerous instrument
notes: Fourth-degree assault is the most common assault charge. Alaska has four degrees of assault. This serves as the simple/misdemeanor assault.

elements: Defendant took property from the person or presence of another
By use of force or threat of force
notes: Second-degree robbery is the base robbery offense. First-degree robbery (AS 11.41.500) involves a deadly weapon, serious injury, or certain other aggravating factors.

elements: Defendant committed robbery
Defendant was armed with a deadly weapon or represented by words or conduct to be so armed
Or caused or attempted to cause serious physical injury
notes: Class A Felony. Includes armed robbery and robbery causing serious injury. Presumptive sentencing ranges apply.

elements: Defendant restrained another person with intent to
Hold for ransom, use as shield or hostage, inflict physical injury, or commit a felony
Or restrained with intent to place the person in involuntary servitude
notes: Unclassified Felony — the most serious felony classification in Alaska. Presumptive term is 10-15 years for first offense.

elements: Defendant intentionally damaged a building by starting a fire or explosion
The building was a dwelling, or the defendant knew people were present
Or intentionally set fire to property that results in damage to a dwelling
notes: First-degree arson involves dwellings or occupied structures. Second-degree arson (AS 11.46.410, Class B Felony) involves non-dwelling buildings.

elements: Defendant intended to cause the death of another person
Defendant engaged in conduct constituting a substantial step toward commission of murder
Conduct was strongly corroborative of the intent
notes: Under Alaska's attempt statute, an attempt is one class below the target offense. Attempted unclassified felony murder is a Class A Felony.

elements: Defendant caused physical injury to another person
By means of a dangerous instrument
With intent to cause physical injury
notes: Second-degree assault covers assault with a dangerous instrument causing physical injury. If serious physical injury results, may be elevated to first degree.

offense_class: Class C Felony ($750-$25,000); Class B Felony (over $25,000)
elements: Defendant obtained or exercised control over property of another
With intent to deprive the owner of the property
enhancements: Theft of a firearm (automatic felony regardless of value)
notes: Theft thresholds: over $25,000 = first degree (Class B Felony), $750-$25,000 = second degree (Class C Felony), under $750 = third degree (Class A Misdemeanor).

elements: Defendant obtained or exercised control over property of another
Value exceeds $25,000
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Alaska uses degree-based theft classifications. First degree is the equivalent of grand theft for property valued over $25,000.

elements: Defendant obtained or exercised control over property of another
Value is less than $750
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Under $750 threshold. Fourth-degree theft (AS 11.46.150) is a Class B Misdemeanor for theft of services under $750.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (under $250); Class A Misdemeanor ($250-$750); felony (over $750)
penalty_max: 90 days (Class B); 1 year (Class A); felony penalties if value warrants
elements: Defendant concealed merchandise of a mercantile establishment on premises
Without paying
With intent to deprive the merchant of the merchandise
notes: Alaska has a specific concealment of merchandise statute. Higher-value shoplifting is charged under the general theft statutes.

elements: Defendant entered or remained unlawfully in a building
With intent to commit a crime in the building
notes: Second-degree burglary covers non-dwelling buildings. First-degree burglary (AS 11.46.300) involves a dwelling.

elements: Defendant entered or remained unlawfully in a dwelling
With intent to commit a crime therein
notes: First-degree burglary requires entry into a dwelling. Dwelling includes any building regularly used for overnight lodging.

elements: Defendant took, drove, or operated a vehicle
Without consent of the owner
With intent to deprive the owner of the vehicle
notes: Alaska has separate vehicle theft statutes. Second-degree vehicle theft (AS 11.46.365) is a Class A Misdemeanor for joyriding without intent to deprive permanently.

offense_class: Class C Felony ($750+); Class A Misdemeanor (under $750)
elements: Defendant received, retained, or disposed of stolen property
Knowing that the property was stolen
Or under circumstances that would cause a reasonable person to believe it was stolen
notes: Degree follows value thresholds similar to theft statutes.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (under $750); Class C Felony ($750-$25,000); Class B Felony (over $25,000)
penalty_max: 1 year (Class A Misdemeanor); 5 years (Class C); 10 years (Class B)
elements: Defendant intentionally damaged property of another
Without consent of the owner
enhancements: Damage to utility or public service property
notes: Alaska uses 'criminal mischief' with five degrees. First degree (AS 11.46.475) is Class A Felony for damage over $100,000.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first degree); Class B Misdemeanor (second degree)
elements: Defendant entered or remained unlawfully on the land or in a building of another
After receiving notice not to trespass
notes: First degree involves a dwelling. Second degree (AS 11.46.330) involves a building or premises.

elements: Defendant intentionally damaged property of another
Damage exceeds $100,000
Or defendant tampered with oil or gas pipelines or production facilities
notes: Damage thresholds determine degree. First: $100,000+. Second: $25,000-$100,000. Third: $750-$25,000. Fourth: under $750 or reckless damage. Fifth: tampering.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (fourth degree); enhanced for repeat offenders
elements: Defendant recklessly caused physical injury to a household member
Household member includes spouse, former spouse, cohabitant, or person sharing a child
enhancements: Two or more prior DV convictions within 10 years (Class C Felony under AS 11.41.220)
notes: Alaska designates DV as a factor, not a separate crime. Any assault charge with a DV designation has enhanced consequences including mandatory arrest, firearm prohibition, and no diversion.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor; Class C Felony (habitual offender with 2+ prior DV convictions within 10 years)
elements: Defendant caused physical injury to a household member
Through reckless conduct or intentional act
enhancements: Prior DV convictions (habitual violator — Class C Felony)
notes: Alaska merged assault and battery. Domestic violence is a designation added to existing assault charges, not a separate offense. Mandatory arrest on probable cause.

statute_title: Endangering the Welfare of a Child — First Degree
elements: Defendant, being a parent, guardian, or other person legally charged with care of a child under 16
Intentionally deserted the child in a place under circumstances creating a substantial risk of physical injury
Or left the child with another knowing the child would be abused
notes: Second-degree endangerment (AS 11.51.110) is a Class A Misdemeanor for failing to provide adequate care.

elements: Defendant intentionally caused serious physical injury to a child under 12
Or recklessly caused serious physical injury to a child under 16
notes: Child abuse is charged under the assault statutes with age of victim as an aggravating factor. Mandatory reporting requirements under AS 47.17.

statute_title: Violation of a Domestic Violence Protective Order
offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (first); Class C Felony (second within 5 years)
elements: A valid domestic violence protective order was in effect
Defendant had notice of the order
Defendant knowingly committed an act in violation of the order
enhancements: Second violation within 5 years (Class C Felony)
notes: First offense is Class A Misdemeanor. Repeat within 5 years becomes Class C Felony. Arrest is mandatory on probable cause.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (second degree); Class C Felony (first degree)
elements: Defendant knowingly engaged in a course of conduct
That recklessly placed another person in fear of death or physical injury
To that person or a family member
enhancements: Violation of protective order while stalking (first degree under AS 11.41.260)
notes: First-degree stalking (AS 11.41.260) is a Class C Felony when committed in violation of a court order or with a prior stalking conviction.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (second degree); Class A Misdemeanor (first degree)
elements: Defendant with intent to harass or annoy another person
Made repeated telephone calls, insults, taunts, or challenges
That were likely to provoke violent or disorderly response
notes: First-degree harassment (AS 11.61.118) involves physical contact or placing a person in fear of physical injury.

elements: Defendant possessed a firearm
While intoxicated or on school grounds
Or discharged a firearm from a motor vehicle
notes: Alaska has five degrees of weapons misconduct. Third degree covers possessing while intoxicated, on school grounds, or discharging from a vehicle.

statute_title: Misconduct Involving Weapons — Third Degree (Felon in Possession)
elements: Defendant possessed a concealable firearm
After having been convicted of a felony or adjudicated as a delinquent minor for a felony-equivalent offense
notes: Applies to concealable firearms only. Alaska's constitutional right to bear arms does not override the felon prohibition. Also charged under federal law 18 U.S.C. § 922(g).

elements: Defendant possessed a deadly weapon other than a firearm
Concealed on their person
Or carried a firearm in a prohibited area
notes: Alaska is a constitutional carry state — no permit required for concealed firearms for those legally permitted to possess. Violations relate to prohibited locations (courthouses, schools, bars).

elements: Defendant knowingly discharged a firearm
At or in the direction of a building
With reckless disregard for risk of physical injury to another
notes: Second-degree weapons misconduct covers reckless discharge. First degree (AS 11.61.190) covers use of a firearm in commission of certain felonies.

offense_class: Class B Felony (over $750); Class C Felony (under $750 or without specific value)
elements: Defendant obtained personal identifying information of another
Without the person's consent
With intent to obtain a benefit, credit, or other thing of value
notes: Covers use of another's name, Social Security number, driver's license number, financial account information, or biometric data.

statute_title: Theft — By Failure to Make Required Disposition of Funds
offense_class: Class B Felony (over $25,000); Class C Felony ($750-$25,000)
elements: Defendant obtained property of another that was entrusted
Defendant failed to make required disposition of the property
With intent to deprive the owner
notes: Charged under general theft statutes. Embezzlement is a theory of theft, not a separate crime in Alaska.

elements: Defendant falsely made, completed, or altered a written instrument
With intent to defraud
The instrument purports to be money, securities, postage, revenue stamps, or government-issued ID
notes: First degree covers government instruments and financial documents. Second degree (AS 11.46.505) covers deeds, wills, and commercial instruments. Third degree (AS 11.46.510) covers other documents.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (under $750); Class A Misdemeanor ($750+)
elements: Defendant issued a check knowing there were insufficient funds
With intent that payment would be refused
Or failed to make good within 15 days of notice of dishonor
notes: Threshold is $750 for felony-level. Defendant gets 15 days after notice of dishonor to make the check good as a defense.

statute_title: Theft by Deception / Scheme to Defraud
offense_class: Class B Felony (scheme to defraud over $750); Class C Felony (theft by deception $750-$25,000)
elements: Defendant obtained property by deception or false pretenses
Or engaged in a scheme to defraud by obtaining property through false representation
notes: Scheme to defraud (AS 11.46.580) is a separate offense from theft by deception. Both require proof of intentional misrepresentation.

statute_title: Fraudulent Use of an Access Device
offense_class: Class C Felony ($750+); Class A Misdemeanor (under $750)
elements: Defendant used an access device (credit card, debit card, etc.)
With intent to defraud
Knowing the device was stolen, forged, canceled, or revoked
notes: Access device includes credit cards, debit cards, account numbers, and electronic fund transfer codes.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual contact with another person
Without the person's consent
By force, threat, or when the person was incapacitated
enhancements: Victim is under 13 (elevated to first degree)
notes: Second-degree covers non-penetrative sexual contact without consent. First-degree (AS 11.41.410) covers sexual penetration.

penalty_min: 8 years (presumptive, no prior felony); 15 years (with prior sexual felony)
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual penetration with another person
Without the person's consent
Through force, threat, or incapacitation
notes: Alaska uses 'sexual assault' rather than 'rape.' Unclassified Felony with substantial presumptive terms. Sex offender registration required.

offense_class: Class B Misdemeanor (second degree); Class A Misdemeanor (first degree)
elements: Defendant knowingly exposed their genitals
In the presence of another person
With reckless disregard for the offensive or alarming effect
enhancements: Exposure to a person under 16 (first degree under AS 11.41.457)
Prior conviction (may require sex offender registration)
notes: First-degree (AS 11.41.457) applies when victim is under 16 or defendant masturbates in presence of another. May trigger sex offender registration.

elements: Defendant engaged in or offered to engage in sexual conduct
In return for a fee
Or solicited a person to engage in sexual conduct for a fee
enhancements: Promoting prostitution (Class C Felony under AS 11.66.120)
notes: Both the seller and buyer can be charged. Promoting prostitution and sex trafficking carry significantly higher penalties.

offense_class: Class B Felony (distribution); Class C Felony (possession under AS 11.61.127)
elements: Defendant distributed, possessed, or produced material depicting a minor under 18 engaged in sexual conduct
Defendant knew or should have known the material depicted a minor
enhancements: Production of material (Class A Felony under AS 11.41.455)
notes: Production is charged under sexual exploitation of a minor (AS 11.41.455), a Class A Felony. Sex offender registration mandatory.

statute_title: Failure to Register as Sex Offender
offense_class: Class C Felony (first); Class B Felony (second+)
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender or child kidnapper
Defendant knowingly failed to register, verify, or update registration as required
notes: Must register within 1 working day of establishing residence. Quarterly in-person verification required. Alaska has some of the most stringent registration requirements.

statute_title: Sexual Abuse of a Minor — Second Degree
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual penetration with a person
Who was 13, 14, or 15 years old
And defendant was at least 4 years older than the victim
enhancements: Victim under 13 (first degree, Class A Felony under AS 11.41.434)
notes: Age of consent in Alaska is 16. Close-in-age exception: no crime if both parties are 13-17 and within 3 years of age. Sex offender registration required.

elements: Defendant with intent to disturb the peace and privacy of another
Engaged in fighting or tumultuous behavior
Or made unreasonable noise, or used offensive words likely to provoke an immediate violent response
notes: Common add-on charge. May be charged with resisting arrest or other public order offenses.

elements: Defendant knowingly resisted or interfered with a person known to be a peace officer
Effecting an arrest or performing an official duty
By force or by committing another act constituting a risk of physical injury
notes: Creating a substantial risk of physical injury while resisting is required for Class A Misdemeanor. Passive resistance may result in lesser charges.

elements: Defendant rendered assistance to a person who committed a felony
With intent to prevent the apprehension, prosecution, or conviction of that person
Assistance included harboring, concealing, providing weapon, or warning of detection
notes: First-degree when assisting a person who committed a felony. Second-degree (AS 11.56.615, Class A Misdemeanor) when assisting a misdemeanor.

offense_class: Varies (civil or criminal; summary or indirect)
elements: Defendant willfully disobeyed a lawful court order
Or engaged in disorderly, contemptuous, or insolent behavior in court
notes: Criminal contempt is punitive. Civil contempt is coercive and continues until the contemnor complies. Right to jury trial for serious criminal contempt.

elements: Defendant was intoxicated in a public place
Defendant's conduct was of a nature to disturb the peace of others
Or defendant was a danger to themselves or others
notes: Alaska decriminalized public intoxication itself — officers should take intoxicated persons to a treatment facility. Criminal charges apply only when behavior rises to disorderly conduct.

offense_class: Class C Felony (felony underlying charge); Class A Misdemeanor (misdemeanor underlying charge)
elements: Defendant was released under the conditions of bail or personal recognizance
Defendant failed to appear in court as required
Failure was without lawful excuse
notes: Bench warrant issued. Bond forfeiture in addition to new criminal charges.

elements: Defendant gave false information to a peace officer
Regarding a crime or emergency
Knowing the information was false
notes: Includes false reports of crimes, false alarms, and providing false identification to police.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (second degree); Class C Felony (first degree)
elements: Defendant made a threat to commit a crime of violence
Or to cause damage to property exceeding $500
With intent to terrorize, intimidate, or cause serious public inconvenience
enhancements: Threat involving explosive or biological agent (first degree under AS 11.56.807)
notes: First-degree terroristic threatening involves threats of mass casualties, explosives, or biological/chemical agents.

elements: Defendant made a false sworn statement
In an official proceeding
The false statement was material
Defendant did not believe the statement was true
notes: Unsworn falsification (AS 11.56.210) is a Class A Misdemeanor. Perjury requires a sworn statement in an official proceeding.

elements: Defendant conferred, offered, or agreed to confer a benefit
Upon a public servant
With intent to influence the public servant's action in an official capacity
notes: Both the briber and the bribed official can be charged. Receiving a bribe (AS 11.56.110) carries the same penalties.

elements: Defendant was in official detention for a felony
Defendant removed himself from that detention without authorization
notes: First degree: escape from felony detention. Second degree (AS 11.56.310, Class B Felony): escape from misdemeanor detention or correctional facility. Third degree (AS 11.56.320): violating conditions of release.

offense_class: Class A Misdemeanor (most acts); Class C Felony (aggravated cruelty)
penalty_max: 1 year (Class A Misdemeanor); 5 years (Class C Felony)
elements: Defendant intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly
Inflicted severe or protracted pain or suffering on an animal
Or failed to provide minimum care for an animal in defendant's custody
notes: Alaska enhanced animal cruelty penalties in recent years. Aggravated cruelty involves intentional torture or killing. Seizure of animals and prohibition on future ownership may be ordered.

penalty_max: Remaining suspended sentence on underlying offense
elements: Defendant was placed on probation
Defendant violated a condition of probation
Violation was willful or without good cause
enhancements: New criminal offense while on probation
notes: Court may revoke, extend, or modify probation. Hearing required. Graduated sanctions may be applied for technical violations. Standard of proof is preponderance of evidence.

elements: Defendant was released on parole
Defendant violated a condition of parole
Violation was established at a hearing
notes: Parole Board makes revocation decisions. Technical violations may result in graduated sanctions. New criminal convictions typically result in full revocation.

elements: Defendant aided, abetted, or encouraged another person
In planning or committing a crime
With intent to promote or facilitate the commission of the offense
notes: An accomplice is guilty to the same degree as the principal. Alaska follows the Model Penal Code approach to complicity.

offense_class: One class below the target offense; Class A Felony max for unclassified felony attempt
penalty_max: Varies — one degree below target offense
fine_max: Varies — one degree below target offense
elements: Defendant intended to commit a crime
Defendant engaged in conduct constituting a substantial step toward commission of the crime
notes: Attempt to commit an unclassified felony is a Class A Felony. Attempt to commit a Class A Felony is a Class B Felony, and so on.

offense_class: One class below the target offense; Class A Felony max for unclassified felony conspiracy
penalty_max: Varies — one degree below target offense
fine_max: Varies — one degree below target offense
elements: Defendant agreed with one or more persons to engage in conduct constituting a crime
Defendant or a co-conspirator committed an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy
notes: Alaska requires an overt act for conspiracy. Renunciation is a defense if the defendant thwarted the success of the conspiracy.
